phonemes.desc: Voiceless glottal [h] followed by the falling diphthong [ɛi] — the 'ei' Old Norse writes with two letters and the runes with one. Stress sits on this first syllable, as in every Old Norse word.
Voiced dental stop [d], short open [ɑ], and the geminate lateral [lː] — the double l is held long, a long consonant the spelling insists on.
The syllabic alveolar trill [r̩] of the nominative ending; the final r carries its own beat, as in modern Icelandic.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAYM-dahl-r' — the ei is the diphthong of 'day', the a short and open, the double l held long, and the final r sounded as a light syllabic trill, as in Icelandic Heimdallur.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods; the first element is heimr, 'world, home'.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Heimdallur, the name's unbroken living form.

kin.label: Norwegian
kin.form: Heimdal, the form carried by place-names — among them the Trondheim borough — and by the modern given name.

kin.label: Modern reception
kin.form: Heimdall, the spelling most of the world now meets first — the watcher at the Bifrost of film and comic.

pronunciation.note: Heimdallr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn, no eth for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The etymology is genuinely debated (heimr 'world, home' plus a disputed second element, usually taken as the rare poetic dallr, perhaps 'bright one'), but the orthography is not: only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Foreknowledge, Watchman, Bifrost
domains.subtitle: The Watchman of Himinbjǫrg and the Horn of Ragnarǫk
domains.lead: Heimdallr is the watchman of the gods: the white god who sits at Himinbjǫrg by the bridge's end, who needs less sleep than a bird, who sees a hundred leagues by night as by day, and who hears the grass grow on the earth and the wool on the sheep. When the end comes it is his horn that wakes the nine worlds — and his last fight, with Loki, that ends them both.

cards.name: The Gjallarhorn
cards.desc: The resounding horn hidden in Mímir's well, whose blast is heard in every world when the last day dawns.

cards.name: Himinbjǫrg
cards.desc: 'Heaven-mountain', the eighth dwelling in Grímnismál's tally, where the watchman drinks good mead beside the bridge's end.

cards.name: Gulltoppr
cards.desc: 'Gold-top', his horse — the mount he rode to Baldr's pyre in Gylfaginning's account of the funeral.

cards.name: Gullintanni
cards.desc: 'Golden-teeth', his byname — Snorri says his teeth were of gold, and the þulur kept the epithet among his names.

symbols.name: The Gjallarhorn
symbols.meaning: The resounding horn hidden beneath the sacred tree — the blast that will be heard in all worlds when the end begins

symbols.name: The golden teeth
symbols.meaning: Gullintanni, the byname Snorri explains plainly — the watchman's brightness struck in metal

symbols.name: Himinbjǫrg
symbols.meaning: 'Heaven-mountain', his hall at the bridge's head — the one dwelling in the Edda defined entirely by the duty kept there

symbols.name: The hearing
symbols.meaning: He hears grass growing on the earth and wool on sheep — vigilance sharpened past the edge of the possible

symbols.name: The green ways of Rígr
symbols.meaning: The roads he walked as Rígr, sleeping three nights in each house — the wanderings that fathered the classes of men

mythology.lead: Heimdallr's myths are scattered across the whole corpus — a stanza here, a þula there, a lost poem behind a kenning — but they add up to a single office: the god who watches, and the horn that ends the watching.

myths.title: The Watchman at Himinbjǫrg
myths.text: Grímnismál counts Himinbjǫrg the eighth of the gods' dwellings, 'and there they say Heimdallr rules over his sanctuaries; there the watchman of the gods drinks, in the peaceful house, gladly, the good mead.' Snorri fills out the portrait in Gylfaginning: Heimdallr is called the white god, and he is great and holy. He dwells at Himinbjǫrg beside Bifrǫst, at heaven's edge, to guard the bridge against the mountain-giants. He needs less sleep than a bird; he sees by night just as well as by day for a hundred leagues; he hears the grass growing on the earth and the wool on sheep, and everything that makes more noise than that. His horn is the Gjallarhorn, and its blast is heard in all worlds. His horse is Gulltoppr, his teeth are of gold, and one of his names — Hallinskiði, 'the slant-horned' — is elsewhere a name for the ram.

myths.title: Born of Nine Mothers
myths.text: Hyndluljóðr gives him the strangest birth in the Edda: 'One was born in days of old, greatly increased in strength, of the gods' kin; nine bore him, that spear-glorious man, giant-maids at the edge of the earth.' The poem names the mothers — Gjálp and Greip, Eistla and Eyrgjafa, Ulfrún and Angeyja, Imðr and Atla and Járnsaxa — and says the child was strengthened with the might of the earth, the ice-cold sea, and sacrificial blood. Snorri quotes the companion lines in Gylfaginning: 'I am the son of nine mothers, I am the son of nine sisters.' Why the watchman of the gods should be the child of nine giantesses is one of the Edda's standing riddles; the poem does not explain, and the scholars have never stopped asking.

myths.title: Rígr and the Three Classes
myths.text: The prose frame of Rígsþula names him outright: 'Men say in old stories that one of the Æsir, who was called Heimdallr, went on his way, and walking along some seashore he came to a farmstead and called himself Rígr.' Three nights he spends between the great-grandparents Ái and Edda, and from that house comes Þræll, the thrall; three nights between Afi and Amma, and from them Karl, the free farmer; three nights between Faðir and Móðir, and from them Jarl, the noble. To Jarl, Rígr returns in person: he teaches him runes, gives him his own name, and declares him his son, bidding him win and rule the ancestral lands. The poem is the Edda's only myth of the making of mankind's classes — and Völuspá's opening address to 'all the sons of Heimdallr, greater and lesser' suggests the tradition meant it: all men are the watchman's children.

myths.title: The Seal-Fight at Singasteinn
myths.text: Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa, quoted in Skáldskaparmál, preserves the oldest Heimdallr myth on record — stanzas from a poem composed about 983: the famed one, wise in counsel, strives at Singasteinn with the cunning son of Fárbauti, and the mighty son of nine mothers holds the fair sea-kidney. The son of Fárbauti is Loki; the 'sea-kidney' is the Brísingamen, Freyja's necklace; and Snorri's prose explains that the two gods had taken the shapes of seals and fought for the jewel in the water. The feud is the oldest thing on record between them: a generation before the Eddas were written down, the skalds already knew that Heimdallr and Loki end up on opposite sides of a fight.

myths.title: The Horn at Ragnarǫk
myths.text: Völuspá gives the end its sound: 'Mímir's sons are at play, and fate is kindled at the old Gjallarhorn; loudly blows Heimdallr, the horn is aloft; Óðinn speaks with Mímir's head.' Snorri stages it in Gylfaginning: Heimdallr stands up and blows the Gjallarhorn with all his strength and wakes all the gods, and they hold their last council. And when the lines form on the field Vígríðr, the oldest enmity in the corpus closes: Loki fights with Heimdallr, and each brings about the other's death. The watchman and the thief — the seal-fight fought once more at the end of the world, and this time neither walks away.

myths.title: The Hearing Under the Tree
myths.text: The strangest of all the Heimdallr stanzas is Völuspá 27: 'She knows Heimdallr's hearing is hidden under the bright-grown sacred tree; she sees it washed by a muddy torrent from the pledge of the Father of the Slain — do you understand yet, or what more?' The pledge of Óðinn is his eye, given to Mímir's well, and Snorri says the Gjallarhorn itself lies hidden in that same well. Whether the völva means the horn or the god's hearing itself — whether Heimdallr pawned an ear to the water as Óðinn pawned an eye — the stanza will not say, and the debate is more than a century old. What is certain is the pairing: the seeing god and the hearing god both paid a sense into the same well.

lore.syncretism: Heimdallr resists the usual syncretic moves — no Roman writer ever matched him, and no continental charm securely names him — but the twentieth century built him a different kind of company. Georges Dumézil made Rígsþula a Scandinavian cornerstone of his trifunctional reading of Indo-European society: thrall, farmer, and noble begotten by one wandering god maps the pattern he traced from the Vedas to Rome. Within the Germanic record, the clearest pairing is the Saltfleetby spindle whorl from Lincolnshire, whose runic charm calls on Óðinn and Heimdallr and Þjálfi for help — the watchman invoked beside the Allfather in a working household. Scholars have also set his nine giantess-mothers beside Ægir's nine wave-daughters and his birth 'at the edge of the earth' beside other shore-born figures; none of the equations has won consensus, and the handbooks converge on the same honest word: enigmatic.
lore.culturalLegacy: Heimdallr's afterlife runs on the horn and the watch. The name never left the North — Norwegian Heimdal survives in place-names and as a given name, and Icelandic keeps Heimdallur — and in modern reception he has become the fixed image of the gatekeeper: the cinema's Heimdall, sighting across the Bifröst, is now the spelling most of the world meets first, and security software borrows the name when it wants to promise that nothing gets past. Modern Heathenry honors him as the father of mankind's orders and the god of vigilance, while the scholarship keeps him as its favorite unsolved problem — the white god whose dossier is large and whose meaning is still debated.
lore.extendedMeditation: Heimdallr is the god of the unglamorous miracle: attention. No adventure of his survives whole — the great deeds are lost poems and kenning-fragments — but the corpus is unanimous about the senses. He hears grass grow. He sees through night. He needs less sleep than a bird. And the Edda builds the whole meaning of vigilance out of that patience: the watch is not the battle; the watch is what makes the battle survivable, and the horn is what makes the watch worth keeping. Rígsþula adds the stranger claim — that this same tireless attention once walked the green ways as Rígr and fathered every class of men, as if to say that society itself began as something watched over. His last act is not a victory: he blows the horn, and then he and Loki kill each other. The watch ends in the warning, not in the rescue. That is the whole of it, and it is enough: someone has to be awake when the rest of the world is not, and the Edda gave that someone a name.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Heimdallr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᛁᛘᛏᛅᛚᛦ (h-i-m-t-a-l-R, the ᛏ writing d, a single ᛚ standing for the geminate, and ᛦ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: heimdallr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Heimdallr's material record is thin but real. The outstanding witness is the Saltfleetby spindle whorl (Lincolnshire, 10th–11th c.), a lead whorl whose runic inscription calls on Óðinn, Heimdallr, and Þjálfi for help — the only runic charm yet found that invokes the watchman by name, and proof his name travelled to England with the Norse settlers. In art, the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria carries a Ragnarǫk panel with a figure raising a horn, often read as Heimdallr sounding the last alarm, and the Jurby cross-slab on the Isle of Man shows a horn-blowing figure sometimes given the same reading; neither stone names him. Place-names formed on his hall Himinbjǫrg survive in Scandinavia (the Himberg type in Norway and Sweden), and Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa — composed about the carvings in Óláfr pái's hall at Hjarðarholt — proves his myth decorated a chieftain's hall by the 980s. Of the texts: the Codex Regius preserves Völuspá, Grímnismál, Þrymskviða, and Lokasenna; Rígsþula survives only in the Codex Wormianus; Hyndluljóðr in Flateyjarbók.
